Waydroid's network stack has three layers: an LXC bridge, NAT, and dnsmasq DHCP. Its security boundary must be checked against the actual Namespace, AppArmor, Seccomp, capabilities, and D-Bus authorization configuration. The mere existence of these mechanisms does not mean that the default environment enables the corresponding isolation.

Waydroid does not create a tap/tun virtual network interface for the Android container. Instead, it creates a Linux bridge named waydroid0 and uses NAT to forward the host network into the container. The full network topology is as follows:
Gateway address, also used for the dnsmasq binding
The container's eth0 obtains an address from this range
Fixed MAC; dnsmasq can use it to assign a fixed IP
Network initialization is performed by /usr/lib/waydroid/waydroid-net.sh (or triggered by the waydroid-net systemd service), in the following order:
Create the bridge: brctl addbr waydroid0, or ip link add waydroid0 type bridge
Configure the host IP: ip addr add <EXAMPLE_IP>/24 dev waydroid0
Bring up the bridge: ip link set waydroid0 up
Set NAT rules: select the iptables or nftables variant for the system environment (see the next section)
Start dnsmasq: listen on the waydroid0 interface to provide DHCP and DNS
Start the container with LXC: LXC creates a veth pair, attaches one end to the bridge, and places the other in the container's namespace
Checking IPv6 compatibility with the network script

Check the IPv6 requirements of the current package and network script Even if you do not use IPv6 networking at all and waydroid0 is IPv4-only, the kernel must enable CONFIG_IPV6=y. This is because the network script or Android networking components may require IPv6 to be available; Binder does not have such a direct dependency on IPv6. Check whether the network script fails because /proc/sys/net/ipv6/ is missing, rather than interpreting a networking requirement as a Binder protocol requirement. The default NixOS kernel already meets this requirement.

nftables integration on NixOS: if your NixOS configuration already declares a networking.nftables ruleset, Waydroid needs the corresponding FORWARD and NAT paths opened in it. You can explicitly add waydroid chains through networking.nftables.ruleset, or use the virtualisation.waydroid module to handle this automatically.

When Docker and Waydroid run on the same system, the docker0 bridge (default <EXAMPLE_IP>/16) may conflict with waydroid0 routes or nftables rules. Typical symptoms include no network access inside the Android container or disrupted Docker container networking.
Android reports a Wi-Fi connection but cannot open web pages
waydroid log reports no errors, but networking fails silently
Docker container networking malfunctions after Waydroid starts

Explanation: with # LXC_USE_NFT=true 属于网络脚本变量，不是此 LXC 配置项, LXC tries to use nftables to create container network rules, which may overwrite or be overwritten by Docker's nftables rules in chains at the same hook priority. Disabling it makes LXC fall back to iptables-legacy. The actual issue may be Docker changing the FORWARD policy, rule ordering, overlapping subnets, or mixed backends. Inspect the actual rules and routes; adding an invalid variable to the LXC config cannot solve the problem.
Even when Waydroid's internal NAT works, the host firewall may still block forwarded traffic on waydroid0. The following covers four common firewall approaches.
General prerequisite: enable kernel IP forwarding

UFW's default FORWARD policy is DROP Ubuntu's UFW sets the FORWARD chain policy to DROP by default. This may leave Waydroid without network access; confirm it using rule counters and logs. Allow only the necessary forwarding with the narrowest scope, then verify the result. Do not treat a global ACCEPT policy as required configuration.
Declarative NixOS configuration (/etc/nixos/configuration.nix or a flake module):

This illustrates how a standalone firewall works; it is not additional default configuration required after enabling Waydroid. Inspect the module-generated rules first. A policy drop on a new forward base chain affects all forwarded traffic, so do not paste it blindly into an existing Docker, VPN, or routing setup. Integrate it with the existing policy and check drops in other chains, ordering, duplicate NAT, and a rollback path.

Waydroid is not a complete sandbox and does not provide QEMU/KVM-level isolation. It relies on multiple layers of Linux kernel security mechanisms for defense in depth.
Waydroid uses LXC to create six namespaces for the Android container, giving it a separate view of the system:
Android system partitions (system.img / vendor.img) are visible only inside the container
Inside the container, ps sees Android init as PID 1
The container has its own eth0, routing table, and iptables
Binder is isolated through device contexts and has a host bridge; this cannot be inferred from the IPC namespace alone
The container's hostname is isolated from the host's
Check the actual lxc.idmap; do not assume that root maps to an unprivileged UID by default

Namespace isolation is not a complete sandbox
All namespaces share the same Linux kernel. A single kernel privilege-escalation vulnerability (CVE) can break through all of the isolation. Waydroid's security boundary is much thinner than KVM's, which provides a separate virtual address space and vCPUs.

LXC uses Seccomp-BPF to configure syscall allowlists/blocklists for the container. Check each item against the actual seccomp file. The bpf/io_uring restrictions in the original notes were not present in the upstream defaults examined:
Bypasses filesystem permission checks to access arbitrary files through inode handles
Not listed in the default seccomp configuration examined; also subject to kernel permission restrictions
Not listed in the default seccomp configuration examined; no claim that it is blocked by default
Hot-replaces the kernel; should never be available inside a container
Seccomp profile location: /var/lib/waydroid/lxc/waydroid/waydroid.seccomp (generated by the LXC template).

In Waydroid's architecture, the user-space SessionManager, running with ordinary-user permissions, does not manipulate privileged resources directly. Operations requiring root, such as starting the container, creating binder nodes, and mounting images, send requests over the D-Bus system bus, with PolicyKit deciding whether to authorize them.
The action categories below retain a custom authorization design; these names are not presented as existing upstream PolicyKit actions:
Requires membership in wheel or explicitly entering a password
Only root and the waydroid user are allowed
Inspect the installed D-Bus/authorization files and service code; do not infer that a file exists from an example action.
Linux capabilities: a minimal privilege set
Container processes receive fine-grained capabilities rather than full root privileges. The minimal set granted to the Waydroid container is:

Check capability restrictions using config_base together with seccomp. The current config_base retains broad privileges including sys_admin, sys_ptrace, and sys_time; do not claim that sys_time is absent by default.

Waydroid is not a complete sandbox
Unlike KVM, Waydroid containers share the host's Linux kernel. This means:
Kernel privilege-escalation vulnerabilities directly affect the container's security boundary
Bugs in the binder driver may be exploited by malicious apps
GPU driver vulnerabilities, exposed through /dev/dri/renderD*, create an additional attack surface
Android applications do not undergo Google Play Protect screening (Waydroid does not come with SafetyNet certification)

Risk levels: when running APKs from untrusted sources, different host/Android/VM combinations cannot be assigned a fixed risk ranking. Consider the shared kernel, device permissions, data mappings, and application sources.
